West African tropical forests are highly vulnerable to human-driven environmental change. They have the highest temperatures and longest dry seasons of all tropical forest systems worldwide. The region is under enormous pressure from a rapidly growing human population and its demands for agricultural production, as well as wood and other forest products. Much of the original native forest cover has been lost, and the remnants are at risk from logging, agricultural encroachment, and wildfires. Our work has documented the increasing susceptibility of West African forests to degradation, developed techniques for monitoring these changes with remote sensing, built models to predict the risk of future degradation and deforestation, and quantitied the long-term impacts of degradation on forest carbon storage.

In West Africa, spatial patterns of active fire detections and burned area are mainly influenced by vegetation, whereas the seasonality and intensity of fires are more strongly associated with climate ([Dwomoh and Wimberly 2017](#tropfor-refs)). Between 2003-2015, fire activity generally decreased in the savanna ecoregions but increased in the forested ecoregions. A broader analyis of forests throughout the moist African tropics also found increasing trends of active fire detections that were associated with increasing temperature, vapor pressure deficit, and deforestation ([Wimberly et al. 2024](#tropfor-refs)). In the tropical forest reserves of Ghana, we found that forest degradation caused by fire and other disturbances increases the risk of subsequent fire, raising concerns that increasing droughts resulting from climate change will catalyze new cycles of wildfire and forest loss ([Dwomoh et al. 2019](#tropfor-refs)). In these forests, degradation occurs through a positive feedback loop of declining canopy cover and increasing fire frequency, eventually leading to the establishment of fire-prone vegetation dominated by grasses and invasive shrubs ([Dwomoh and Wimberly 2017](#tropfor-refs)).

Across the Upper Guinean Region of West Africa, we have documented broad trends of decreasing woody vegetation and increasing herbaceous vegetation cover ([Liu et al. 2017](#tropfor-refs)). Using a time series analysis of Landsat imagery, we developed a historical database of disturbances across all forest reserves of Ghana from 2003 to 2019 ([Wimberly et al. 2022](#tropfor-refs)). Rates of forest degradation, loss, and recovery were relatively low from 2003 to 2015, followed by a sharp increase associated with drought and fires in 2016. Patterns of forest disturbance are highly sensitive to landscape fragmentation, human population pressure, and drought, and these variables can be used to map the relative risk of future disturbances ([Wanyama et al. 2023](#tropfor-refs)). Biomass recovery following forest degradation is relatively slow because changes in forest structure increase the potential for subsequent fires and other disturbances ([Wanyama et al. 2025](#tropfor-refs)).
